Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
I try to erase the memory of the event
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette: Ana María still remembers the feeling of being trapped in her childhood home, with no escape from the physical abuse inflicted by her caregiver. She recalls the sound of the door slamming shut behind her, the way the sunlight streaming through the window seemed to mock her as she was pinned against the wall. The memory is fragmented - some moments etched in vivid detail, while others remain shrouded in a haze. When it suddenly surfaces, unbidden and unwelcome, Ana María's mind struggles to process the emotions that come flooding back. As a community organizer, Ana María has dedicated her life to helping others navigate systems of power and find their voice. Yet, despite her professional successes, she often feels like she's just going through the motions. The numbness she experiences when recalling the traumatic event has seeped into other areas of her life, leaving her feeling "dead inside." She wonders if others would have been able to stop the abuse from happening - a thought that haunts her and fuels her self-doubt. In an attempt to regain a sense of control, Ana María has developed certain habits. She always sits with her back against a wall, scanning the room for potential threats. At community meetings, she positions herself near the door, ready to make a quick exit if needed. Her partner, Luis, has noticed these behaviors and tries to reassure her that everything will be okay, but Ana María can't shake off the feeling of vulnerability. To keep her mind occupied and avoid dwelling on the traumatic event, Ana María throws herself into work or tasks. She often finds herself checking emails and responding to messages late into the night, using the distraction as a coping mechanism. This overworking has taken a toll on her relationship with Luis, who feels like he's losing his partner to her all-consuming job. Ana María's difficulty falling asleep is another manifestation of her hypervigilance. She lies awake at night, listening for any unusual sounds that might indicate someone is lurking outside their apartment. Even during the day, she catches herself frequently looking over her shoulder, as if expecting someone to be following her. Luis has tried to reassure her that they live in a safe neighborhood, but Ana María's mind won't let go of the fear. One of the most painful aspects of Ana María's experience is the sense of weakness that lingers long after the traumatic event itself. She believes she should have been stronger, more resilient - that someone else would have found a way to stop the abuse from happening. This self-blame has become a constant companion, whispering in her ear and eroding her confidence. Ana María's struggles with PTSD have finally brought her to seek help. The realization that she can't continue living like this, constantly on edge and plagued by intrusive memories, has prompted her to reach out for support. As she begins therapy, Ana María hopes to learn new coping mechanisms and find a way to quiet the voice of self-doubt that has haunted her for so long. She fears that confronting her past will be too overwhelming, but she's willing to take that risk in order to reclaim her life and find a sense of peace.
